reading.body:
CyrusOne Florence publishes 5 MW of IT capacity, making it Kentucky's largest disclosed facility, though this remains modest against the power budgets now required for frontier AI model training.

Kentucky's three published capacity declarations across five mapped sites total 9.55 MW. CyrusOne Florence accounts for roughly half of this disclosed compute footprint in the state. At standard AI densities, the 143,000 square feet of technical space translates to approximately 125 racks at 40 kW per rack, or roughly 17 pods at 300 kW per accelerator pod. The facility carries compliance certifications spanning regulated workloads: PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FISMA, and SSAE 16 Type II.

The 5 MW figure sits well below single-site capacity at large cloud platforms and far below the power draw of current frontier model training clusters. For AI scaling to depend on grid capacity, this facility would need to expand or operate at exceptionally high utilization. Most Kentucky data center capacity remains unpublished, so the state's actual computational infrastructure is largely invisible.

Whether this site matters to AI infrastructure depends entirely on what is not disclosed: tenant workload composition, actual power draw versus published capacity, utilization rates, and grid interconnection constraints. The operator publishes IT capacity but not applied power, enabling no assessment of whether the facility constrains or supports AI compute expansion.
